Kim Carr The first area we go to is the question of reducing the enrolment period before the closure of the roll to three days. This proposal is necessary to maintain the status quo. The opposition’s concerns with this legislation go to the fact that, in essence, this is a device by which the government is seeking to restrict the franchise. We say that the bill is aimed at restricting the capacity of Australians to participate in the political system and, as a consequence, it will have the effect of undermining the legitimacy of the electoral system. We argue that the net effect of the changes that restrict access to the roll, by reducing the period of time in which people can re-enrol, may well have the effect of disadvantaging some 430,000 people. Four hundred and thirty thousand Australians may lose their capacity to vote as a result of the actions of this government. Our concern is that, essentially, those are the people who need government the most: the homeless; people who are poor; people who are moving constantly, particularly renters; people who are migrants; people who live in distressed economic circumstances; people who tend to be least engaged in the political system. As a consequence of this government’s actions, their participation in the political system will be restricted. We also maintain that they are people who are most likely to vote Labor. speeches.speaker: Rod Kemp
speeches.brief: The bills were introduced together, with a motion to list them separately on the Notice Paper after the second reading debate is adjourned. The motion to proceed without formalities and read the bills a first time was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Rod Kemp
speeches.brief: The speaker introduced bills to raise the political donation disclosure threshold from $1,500 to $10,000, disenfranchise all prisoners serving full-time sentences, extend the Export Market Development Grants scheme to 2010‑11, and replace the general exemption in the Age Discrimination Act with a limited list of exemptions.

speeches.speaker: Kim Carr
speeches.brief: Labor moved to withdraw the Electoral and Referendum Amendment (Electoral Integrity and Other Measures) Bill 2006 unless undemocratic provisions are removed, arguing that reducing the enrolment period, introducing proof-of-identity requirements, raising the disclosure threshold to $10,000 (potentially $80,000 via multiple donations), and increasing tax deductibility of donations would disenfranchise 80,000 new voters and 255,000 address changes every election while enabling secret donations that undermine transparency.

Senator Carr moved an amendment to withdraw the bill until provisions were removed that reduce enrolment time, introduce proof-of-identity requirements, increase disclosure thresholds to $10,000, and increase tax-deductibility of political donations.

speeches.speaker: Kerry O'Brien
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Electoral and Referendum Amendment (Electoral Integrity and Other Measures) Bill 2006 would disenfranchise young people, renters, and Indigenous Australians by requiring enrolment applications to be witnessed by non-relatives and by closing the roll early. The speaker also criticised the increase in the donation disclosure threshold from $1,500 to $10,000, calling it a partisan move to reduce transparency.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Electoral and Referendum Amendment (Electoral Integrity and Other Measures) Bill 2006, arguing that raising the donation disclosure threshold from $1,500 to $10,000 and closing electoral rolls early on the day writs are issued would disenfranchise voters and benefit the Liberal Party, citing a lack of evidence for electoral fraud and the risk of excluding new citizens, 17–18-year-olds, and regional Australians.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Murray
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the government's bill to remove prisoner voting rights, citing human rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and also opposed raising the political donation disclosure threshold from $1,500 to $10,000.

speeches.speaker: John Hogg
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that increasing the political donation disclosure threshold to $10,000 would allow companies and groups to donate large sums without public scrutiny, citing examples of potential undisclosed donations of up to $170,000. The speaker also proposed banning foreign donations and loans to political parties, and requiring third-party electoral advertisers to disclose their funders and relationships.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Murray
speeches.brief: Senator Milne argued that the government's electoral bill fails to require third-party advertisers to register and disclose donors, citing the Tasmanian example where "Tasmanians for a Better Future" spent over $200,000 anonymously. She also criticised the bill for not capturing multiple donations under $10,000 and for allowing secretive groups like the Exclusive Brethren to influence elections without transparency.

speeches.speaker: Bob Brown
speeches.brief: The Family First senator argued that tax deductibility for political donations should be abolished, claiming political parties are self-interested groups not deserving of charity-like treatment. The Greens and Democrats supported the amendment, while Labor and the Coalition opposed it, and the amendment was ultimately defeated.

speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The senator moved to refer the issue of third-party involvement in electoral advertising to the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters, arguing that current disclosure laws allow donations under $10,000 to be hidden through front groups. The senator cited examples from Tasmania, including Concerned Citizens for Tasmania and Tasmanians for a Better Future, and named individuals such as Robin Gray, Gunns Ltd, and Corporate Communications.
